t: Matrix Cells in Distance Order — Editorial
o: We must list every cell of a rows x cols grid, ordered by Manhattan distance from a given center cell (rCenter, cCenter). Ties may be broken arbitrarily. For example 2 with center (0,1): (0,1) has distance 0, (0,0) and (1,1) have distance 1, and (1,0) has distance 2 — so any order grouping cells by those distances is valid. With rows, cols <= 100 there are at most 10,000 cells, so even an O(n log n) sort over all cells is trivially fast; no clever geometry is required.
k: Manhattan distance |r1-r2| + |c1-c2| can be computed directly per cell, no special structure needed.
With at most 10^4 cells, sorting all cells by distance is well within limits.
BFS from the center naturally visits cells in nondecreasing Manhattan-distance order, giving an O(n) alternative.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort All Cells by Distance
a.i: Generate every cell in the matrix, compute its Manhattan distance to the center, and sort the list by that distance. Since ties can be broken arbitrarily, a plain sort on the distance key suffices and the result is always valid.
s: Build a list of all coordinates [r, c] for r in [0, rows), c in [0, cols).
Compute dist = |r - rCenter| + |c - cCenter| for each cell.
Sort the list ascending by dist.
a.t: O(n log n) where n = rows * cols — generating cells is O(n) and sorting dominates.
a.sp: O(n) to store all cells (plus O(log n) or O(n) sort auxiliary space depending on language).

a.n: Approach 2: Counting Sort / Bucket by Distance
a.i: The maximum possible Manhattan distance is bounded by (rows-1) + (cols-1), so we can bucket cells by their exact distance instead of comparison-sorting. Placing each cell into bucket d = its distance and concatenating buckets 0..maxD yields a valid answer in linear time.
s: Let maxD = (rows - 1 - rCenter) + (cols - 1 - cCenter) ... more simply (rows - 1) + (cols - 1).
For every cell, append it to bucket |r - rCenter| + |c - cCenter|.
Concatenate buckets in increasing distance order and return.
a.t: O(rows * cols) — each cell is placed in a bucket once and read once; no comparison sort.
a.sp: O(rows * cols) for the buckets and output.

w: In an interview, lead with the simple sort (Approach 1) since it's one line of logic per language and clearly correct; then mention the counting-sort optimization if asked to beat O(n log n). Pitfalls: forgetting that tie order is arbitrary (any stable/unstable order passes), off-by-one in the maximum distance bound ((rows-1)+(cols-1)), and returning tuples vs lists in Python (lists are expected). Edge cases: 1x1 grid returns just the center; center on a corner maximizes distances. Likely follow-ups: solve without extra memory beyond output (in-place index sort by key), or handle huge grids where only k nearest cells are needed (use a heap or BFS truncated after k cells).
